indiaMissions/india-american-missions/ti: American missions: Madura, Arcot (the Scudders), Ahmednagar
indiaMissions/india-american-missions/su: American Protestant missions began in India in 1813 when the first American Board (ABCFM) missionaries landed in Calcutta and moved to Bombay. Over the next century the American Board built the Marathi mission centred on Ahmednagar and the Madura mission in Tamil Nadu, the Scudder family founded the Reformed Church's Arcot mission and pioneered medical work, and American Presbyterians, Methodists, Baptists and Lutherans spread across north and south India — bringing their own democratic, voluntarist style along with schools, colleges, hospitals and a characteristic hostility to caste.
indiaMissions/india-american-missions/st:
The first American missionaries to India — Adoniram and Ann Judson, Samuel Newell, Samuel Nott, Gordon Hall and Luther Rice — sailed in 1812 under the newly formed American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions (ABCFM), arriving at Calcutta during the war of 1812 between Britain and the United States. The Company ordered them to leave: the Judsons and Rice became Baptists and went to Burma, while Hall and Nott slipped away to Bombay in 1813, where they were threatened with deportation until the governor, Sir Evan Nepean, allowed them to stay in 1815. The Bombay (later Marathi) mission opened schools and printed Marathi scripture; it expanded to Ahmednagar in 1831, which became its main centre. The Ahmednagar church developed relatively strong Indian leadership, organised congregations under Indian pastors from the 1850s, and later produced figures such as the poet Narayan Vaman Tilak.

In 1816 the ABCFM opened a mission in Jaffna, Ceylon, where its Batticotta Seminary trained Tamil Christians; from there missionaries crossed to Madurai in 1834 to found the Madura mission. Its stations at Madurai, Dindigul, Periyakulam, Tirumangalam and elsewhere spread through the Tamil hinterland. The mission insisted, unlike the Tanjore Lutherans, that converts and church workers renounce caste distinctions, and in 1847 it required its agents to show this by eating food prepared by people of other castes — provoking the withdrawal of many higher-caste Christians. Converts came largely from the Shanar (Nadar), Paraiyar and Pallar communities and some Maravar and Kallar villages. The mission opened the Pasumalai seminary (1842), which grew into the American College, Madurai (1881), and a hill station at Kodaikanal (1845) that later housed the Kodaikanal International School (1901).

The Scudder family became the best-known American missionary dynasty in India. Dr John Scudder Sr (1793–1855), a New York physician, went to Ceylon in 1819 as the ABCFM's first medical missionary and moved to Madras in 1836; his tracts and visits to the United States inspired many young Americans. Seven of his sons became missionaries in India. In 1853–54 his sons, led by Henry Martyn Scudder, organised the Arcot mission in the North Arcot district under the Reformed (Dutch) Church in America, with stations at Arcot, Vellore, Chittoor, Madanapalle and Arni. The Arcot mission combined preaching tours, village schools and medical work; its theological seminary (1887) and high schools trained Tamil and Telugu Christian leaders. Ida Scudder (1870–1960), John Sr's granddaughter, founded the women's medical work at Vellore in 1900 that became the Christian Medical College.

The American Board's leadership also shaped mission theory. In 1854–55 its secretary Rufus Anderson visited India and, with Henry Venn of the CMS, championed the 'three-self' ideal of self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating churches. His deputation pressed the Marathi and Madura missions to cut back English education, close some boarding schools and ordain Indian pastors for village churches — a policy welcomed by some Indian Christians as a step to autonomy but resented by others who valued English schooling as a route to advancement.

Other American churches followed. The Presbyterian Church in the USA founded its Lodiana (Ludhiana) mission in 1834, the first in the Punjab, and later Forman Christian College in Lahore (1864). The Methodist Episcopal Church sent William Butler, who began at Bareilly in 1856, just before the uprising of 1857; the mission later spread across north India under James Thoburn, and Isabella Thoburn opened a girls' school at Lucknow in 1870 that became Isabella Thoburn College (1886), the first Christian women's college in Asia. American Baptists took up the Telugu 'Lone Star' mission at Nellore (1840) and Ongole (1866), and the Lutheran 'Father' J. C. F. Heyer began at Guntur in 1842. By the early twentieth century American missionaries, many recruited through the Student Volunteer Movement, were among the largest foreign contingents in India.

American missions contributed strongly to education, medicine and women's work, and their congregational and democratic instincts encouraged Indian church self-government. They also shared the paternalism of their age: Indian pastors were paid far less than missionaries and long kept out of mission councils, and American mission compounds created dependencies that outlasted independence. Most of these missions were absorbed into the Church of South India (1947) — including the Madura and Arcot churches — and the Church of North India (1970), while Methodist, Baptist and Lutheran churches remained separate.

indiaMissions/india-american-missions/le: American missions brought to India a distinctive blend of revivalist zeal, democratic church order, women's work and institution-building. Their colleges and hospitals remain among India's best known, and their three-self theory shaped the push towards Indian church independence, even as their wealth and paternalism created dependencies that Indian churches later had to unwind.

indiaMissions/india-mass-movements/title: Dalit mass movements (Punjab Chuhras, Andhra Malas and Madigas, 1870–1930)
indiaMissions/india-mass-movements/summa: Between about 1870 and 1930 hundreds of thousands of Dalits — Chuhras in the Punjab, Madigas and Malas in the Telugu country, Chamars in north India and others — joined Christian churches in group or 'mass' movements, usually through kinship networks and Indian lay evangelists rather than missionary preaching. These movements transformed Indian Christianity into a predominantly Dalit church, raised literacy and dignity among the converts, provoked fierce debate among missionaries, Hindu reformers and Gandhi, and were analysed in J. Waskom Pickett's landmark Christian Mass Movements in India (1933).
indiaMissions/india-mass-movements/story:
Missionaries had long hoped to convert India through its elites, but from the 1870s the decisive growth came from the bottom of the caste order. Group conversion was not new — the Paravars in the sixteenth century and the Nadars of Tirunelveli in the early nineteenth had joined churches as communities — but the scale was. Dalit communities, regarded as 'untouchable' and held in agricultural servitude, often decided collectively, through kin and caste councils, to accept baptism. Their motives combined religious conviction, the search for dignity and education, protection from landlords, and the hope of escaping the stigma of untouchability; missionaries were frequently surprised and divided by the movements.

In the Punjab the movement began with Ditt, a short, lame Chuhra (hereditary sweeper and agricultural labourer) who dealt in hides in the Sialkot district. In 1873 he sought baptism from the United Presbyterian missionary Samuel Martin at Sialkot and, refusing to stay at the mission, went back to his village and brought his relatives to faith. Through Chuhra kinship networks the movement spread across Sialkot, Gujranwala, Gurdaspur and Lahore districts, involving the United Presbyterian, American Presbyterian, CMS, Church of Scotland, Methodist and Salvation Army missions. Within a few decades most Chuhras of the central Punjab districts had become Christians, and the Punjab church — which had numbered only a few thousand Indian Christians in 1881 — grew into a community of several hundred thousand by 1931, overwhelmingly of Chuhra origin. The Punjabi Zabur, a metrical psalter in Punjabi folk tunes (completed 1908), became the heart of their worship.

In the Telugu country the American Baptist 'Lone Star' mission at Nellore had nearly been abandoned before John E. Clough founded the Ongole station in 1866 and found a responsive Madiga community, partly through the Madiga leader Yerraguntla Periah. During the great famine of 1876–78 Clough took a government contract to dig part of the Buckingham Canal, employing thousands of famine-stricken people, and refused baptism until relief was over. When baptisms resumed, 2,222 people were baptised on 3 July 1878 at Velampalli on the Gundlakamma river, and around nine thousand within a few weeks; the Ongole church became for a time one of the largest Baptist churches in the world. Malas and Madigas also joined Lutheran (Guntur, Rajahmundry), CMS (Ellore, Masulipatnam), SPG, LMS (Cuddapah) and Methodist (Hyderabad, Medak) missions. In the Anglican diocese of Dornakal, founded in 1912 under V. S. Azariah, the first Indian Anglican bishop, Mala and Madiga movements produced a church of more than two hundred thousand by the 1930s, while the Wesleyan Charles Posnett's work among Malas and Madigas led to the building of Medak Cathedral (1914–24) partly as famine-relief employment.

In north India the Methodist Episcopal mission, under Bishop James Thoburn, baptised large numbers of Chamars, Mazhabi Sikhs and Balmikis in Rohilkhand and the Punjab from the 1880s, sometimes with minimal instruction, drawing criticism from other missions. Parallel movements among Adivasi peoples — the Oraons and Mundas of Chota Nagpur through the Gossner and Jesuit missions, and peoples of the north-east — added further numbers. Census figures show the scale of change: India's Christian population rose from about 2.9 million in 1901 to about 6.3 million in 1931, with much of the Protestant growth coming through these movements.

The movements generated intense controversy. Many missionaries feared 'unready' converts and inadequate teaching; others defended group conversion as the natural Indian pattern. Arya Samaj reformers in the Punjab answered with shuddhi reconversion campaigns, and the politics of numbers under separate electorates sharpened tension. Mahatma Gandhi in the 1930s opposed missionary efforts among 'Harijans', arguing that they could not understand the change of religion and that conversion divided Hindu society; he clashed on this with missionary leaders and with B. R. Ambedkar, who in 1935 declared he would not die a Hindu and was courted by Christian, Muslim, Sikh and Buddhist leaders before choosing Buddhism in 1956.

In 1928 the National Christian Council commissioned the American Methodist J. Waskom Pickett to survey the movements. His Christian Mass Movements in India (1933) found that converts in group movements generally showed real improvements in literacy, health, cleanliness and freedom from fear, and that group conversion produced more stable churches than isolated individual conversions. The study shaped Azariah's and others' strategy and inspired Donald McGavran's Church Growth theory. Yet the movements also left lasting problems: Dalit Christians often remained landless labourers, faced violence and boycott, and encountered caste discrimination within the churches themselves, while after independence the Presidential Order of 1950 excluded Christian Dalits from Scheduled Caste benefits.

indiaMissions/india-mass-movements/legac: The Dalit mass movements are the main reason Indian Christianity today is largely a church of Dalits and Adivasis. They brought education and dignity to communities long excluded, but also set the terms of continuing controversies — over motives for conversion, caste within the church and the denial of Scheduled Caste rights to Dalit Christians — that remain central to Indian public life.
